newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/yen looks past Fed to Japan for push above 125.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen looks past Fed to Japan for push above 125.

text.p: Dollar bulls will look beyond an anticipated Federal Reserve interest rate hike this week to future developments in Japan for fresh provocation to thrust the currency above the 125 yen threshhold, U.S. analysts said.
"The momentum for further dollar gains or a push through 125 is going to have to come from their side of the Pacific," said Brian McCarthy, market analyst at Ruesch International.

McCarthy is among the majority of analysts who expect a Fed hike on Tuesday. He said that once that is out of the way, the dominant theme should become U.S./Japan bilateral trade unless the upcoming "tankan" survey is weak.

If U.S. economic data indicate over time that this rate hike is not the last, then that is a different story, McCarthy added. But for the next month or so, direction for trading the dollar is going to have to come from Tokyo.
Japan's quarterly "tankan" survey due on April 2 could provide some direction as a key gauge of corporate sentiment which is closely watched for clues to Japan's monetary policy.

The Bank of Japan has kept official rates at rock bottom levels to help stimulate economic growth. Japan's official discount rate has remained at 0.5 percent, well below the 5.25 percent target rate for federal funds.
The powerful dollar rally has stalled just below 125 yen after the currency briefly hit 124.82 on February 14.

Fed policymakers meet on Tuesday to decide whether to tighten credit to head off inflation. Last week, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments during a testimony to Congress' Joint Economic Committee appeared to hint the central bank is inching toward a rate hike.
Some experts said the market has priced in a rate increase and the dollar could weaken on Tuesday in a classic buy-on-the-rumor-sell-on-the-news reaction if the Fed tightens.
Close on the heels of the Fed policymakers meeting comes the end of Japan's fiscal year on March 31 and the "tankan".
"As we get past fiscal year end, we should start seeing a pick-up in capital outflows from Japan," said Ron Leven, a currency strategist at J.P. Morgan.
"So what's going to cause the dollar to go up is the Japanese investors love our market, and if they don't like our market, the dollar won't go up," he added.
Leven said the dollar will likely break above 125 yen in the next six weeks.
Still, some analysts wondered whether Japan would allow its currency to weaken further and risk the displeasure of the Clinton Administration.
U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky on Friday warned Japan not to "export its way" out of recession.
